scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the parents in this scenario are being AITA (Ask if I'm the Asshole). Let me break it down step by step. First, the parents have a 17-year-old son who suddenly wants to see a therapist. They're surprised because he's always been a normal, active kid with lots of friends. They ask him why, but he doesn't want to say. They're worried, so they send him to a therapist, who he now sees once a week. The parents don't see any obvious issues, so they start speculating—maybe he's bulimic or anorexic, but he's not that skinny, and those issues are more common in women. They also think about depression, but that doesn't seem likely either. Since they can't figure it out on their own, they approach the therapist to ask why their son is going. The therapist refuses, citing confidentiality. The parents insist, wanting at least the reason, not the specifics. The therapist still refuses. The next day, their son finds out they were pushing the therapist and gets upset, insulting them and not talking to them the rest of the day. Now, the parents are questioning if they were wrong to insist on knowing. They feel they deserve to know as his parents but are now dealing with the fallout. So, is it right or wrong for them to insist on knowing why their son is seeing a therapist? I think about the balance between a parent's right to know and their child's privacy. At 17, the son is almost an adult, so his privacy rights are more significant. Therapists are bound by confidentiality, which is important for trust in the therapeutic relationship. If the parents push too hard, they might be overstepping and causing their son to feel betrayed or misunderstood. The parents' intentions are good—they're worried and want to help. But their approach might be too intrusive. They tried to think of possible issues, which is understandable, but when they couldn't find answers, they turned to the therapist. Insisting on knowing despite the therapist's refusal could be seen as not respecting their son's privacy. The consequence was their son getting upset and pulling away, which isn't helpful for communication or his well-being. It might have made him feel that his parents don't trust him or respect his decisions. So, while the parents' concern is valid, their method of getting information was probably wrong. They should have considered their son's privacy and perhaps communicated their concerns in a different way, without pushing the therapist. Maybe talking to their son directly about their worries instead of going through the therapist would have been better. In the end, they might have been a bit too pushy, which led to their son feeling insulted and distant. So, yes, they might be the assholes in this situation, but with good intentions that went about it the wrong way.
